analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers and HMOs to spend at least 85% of premiums on actual patient care.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2000 by Senator Feinstein with zero cosponsors, the bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced every managed care health plan — employer plans, individual insurance, Medicaid HMOs, federal employees' plans, military-family plans, and private Medicare plans — to pay out at least 85 cents of every premium dollar in actual medical benefits. Administrative costs like executive pay, marketing, interest, and office costs could not be counted as care, so overhead and profit together would be capped at 15% of premiums. Plans that failed could face federal fines, and private Medicare plans could have enrollment or payments suspended.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in managed care plans of every kind: employer plans, individual policies, Medicaid HMOs, federal employee plans, military family plans, and private Medicare plans. Each premium dollar would have to buy more actual health care, and the government could investigate complaints and penalize plans that shortchanged benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with managed care health insurance

how_it_helps.text: Each managed care plan would have to ensure that the actuarial value of benefits provided to enrollees is at least 85% of total premium payments received each contract year.

Costs of managing and operating a plan — including compensation and benefits, interest, facility occupancy, and marketing — could not be counted toward that 85%, capping overhead plus profit at 15% of premiums.

The rules would cover not just commercial insurance but Medicaid managed care organizations, federal employee plans, coverage for armed forces members and families, and Medicare+Choice (private Medicare) plans.

The Health and Human Services Secretary would have to set up formal investigation and compliance procedures for complaints, and could impose civil money penalties — up to $25,000 per determination, or $100,000 for misrepresentation — and suspend enrollment or payments for private Medicare plans that substantially fail to comply.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs, whose combined administrative spending and profit would be capped at 15% of premium revenue. Costs that now go to executive compensation, marketing, interest, and building occupancy would have to be redirected to patient benefits or absorbed as lower margins.

drawbacks.text: The penalties are small relative to the size of large insurers: at most $25,000 per determination, or $100,000 where a plan misrepresented or falsified information, which may not be enough to change behavior at large companies.
Enforcement is complaint-driven and starts with giving the plan a chance to write a corrective action plan, with notice and a hearing before any sanction — so relief for enrollees could be slow.

Plans whose solvency is in jeopardy, or for whom compliance would break state licensing solvency rules, could get 12-month waivers, renewable up to 24 months in any 36-month period, delaying the benefit guarantee for those enrollees.

A hard 85% payout floor can squeeze thin-margin plans — generally, strict medical loss ratio rules can push smaller insurers out of a market or into withdrawal, which can reduce choice for consumers in some areas. This is a standard objection to such caps, based on how insurance markets work rather than on anything in the bill's record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — requiring insurers to deliver most of every premium dollar as care rather than overhead and profit — is a substantial consumer protection, and a similar medical loss ratio requirement for insurers was later written into the 2010 health care law, which suggests the approach proved workable. This version's design was weaker in places: modest fines, complaint-based enforcement rather than routine audits, and solvency waivers. But its biggest weakness was political: it attracted no cosponsors and never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Feinstein introduced the bill on July 27, 2000, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and it sat there with no cosponsors and no further action until that Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 27, 2000, and read twice.
It was referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — appears in the record before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and HMOs are better off, because no requirement ever took effect obligating them to spend 85% of premiums on care. Enrollees' premiums continued to be spent under the pre-existing rules, with no cap on how much went to administration and profit.

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Managed Care Integrity Act of 2000 on July 27, 2000 and delivered introductory remarks.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 27, 2000 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never recorded; the only recorded sponsor was a Democrat with zero cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would cap combined overhead and profit at 15% of premiums by requiring 85% of premium revenue to go to actual benefits, excluding executive pay, marketing, interest, and occupancy costs from the calculation. Its gain in being stopped is the absence of any payout floor, which is money that stays with insurers rather than going to enrollees' care.

Private Medicare plans would face the same 85% payout requirement, backed by the stronger remedies of suspended enrollment or suspended payments if they substantially failed to comply. The bill dying left their overhead and margins uncapped.

The bill would have explicitly brought Medicaid HMOs under the 85% payout rule, tightening what they can keep from largely tax-funded premium payments. The cost falls partly on the companies and partly on state programs' contracting flexibility.
